knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

```{r}
library(tidymarkers)
library(knitr)
```

## Four questions for an assay

1. **Can it be designed at all?** — did a `marker_assay` or a `marker_doomed`
   come back.
2. **Is it specific?** — `marker_design_checks()` (the table "criterion / observed
   / limit / pass").
3. **How well does it discriminate the alleles?** — `discrimination` (the
   `DECIPHER` efficiency).
4. **Does structure get in the way?** — dimers/hairpins and 3' stability.

Every answer is a row in a table, not a spoken conclusion: so the same assay can
be compared with another and that comparison can itself be tested.

## Verdict by criterion

`marker_design_checks()` returns a tidy table; a "good" assay passes **all** the
applicable rows. The thresholds live in `KASP_LIMITS` — they are visible and can
be overridden.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
chk <- marker_design_checks(assay)
chk
chk[!chk$pass, c("stage", "criterion", "observed", "limit", "status")]
passes_all(assay)                # TRUE / FALSE in one line
marker_risk(assay)               # low / medium / high + the list of failures
```

The `status` column is the main one, not `pass`:

| `status` | meaning |
|---|---|
| `pass` | measured and within the limit |
| `fail` | measured and outside it — this is the "why it did not pass" |
| `unknown` | could not be measured (no data, tool unavailable) |
| `not_applicable` | the criterion does not apply to this scheme |

`pass` is deliberately `FALSE` for `unknown` and `not_applicable`: "no evidence"
is not the same as "evidence in favour". So filter by `status`, and take `pass`
as a quick answer to "is everything demonstrated".

Criteria: amplicon size, AS/COM Tm (and `COM Tm >= AS Tm`), GC, homopolymers,
SSR, hairpin/cross- and homodimer, discrimination, in-silico PCR (REF=1, ALT=0).

## Plan → run → export

A single locus is assembled by `assemble_kasp_assay()`. A panel of loci and the
choice of chemistry are a plan: targets (`marker_targets()`), context
(`marker_context()`) and the available technologies (`marker_tech()`), then
`marker_solve()`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plan <- marker_plan(genome) +
  marker_targets(marker_example("snp")) +
  marker_context(variants = variants) +
  marker_tech(preset = "lab")           # kasp / gel / lab / field

solved <- marker_solve(plan, progress = FALSE)
solved
```

`<marker_solved>` prints a "target × chemistry" report, and the object itself
carries three layers:

| Layer | What is inside |
|---|---|
| `solved$report` | one row per locus: `label`, `scheme`, `cost`, `ok`, `tried`, `marker` |
| `solved$attempts` | one row per (locus, chemistry) pair: what was tried and how it ended |
| `solved$report$marker` | the objects themselves — `marker_assay` or `marker_doomed` |

`ok` means "a marker object came back", and **not** "passed all checks": the
acceptance criteria live in `$evaluation`, and an assay with a failure stays in
the report (see "Why a candidate did not pass" below).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
solved$report[, c("label", "scheme", "cost", "ok", "tried")]
solved$attempts
marker_plot(solved)                     # tiles: which chemistry took the locus
solved$report$marker[[1]]
```

The solver goes **from cheap chemistry to expensive** and stops at the first one
that designed the locus, so `attempts` is also the answer to "why KASP and not
CAPS": everything to the left of the winning row was cheaper and did not work.
`marker_solve(..., all = TRUE)` runs the whole matrix, and `cache =` allows
loci already computed to be reused between calls.

### Exporting the object

`solved` is an ordinary R object, and it serialises whole:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
dir <- marker_export(solved, dir = "results/solved")
fs::dir_ls(dir)
# markers.csv    attempts.csv    primers.csv    solved.rds
# artefact.json  decisions.csv   checks.csv      targets.csv
```

- `markers.csv` — the per-locus report;
- `attempts.csv` — the attempt matrix;
- `primers.csv` — the oligos of every solved marker (`target`, `scheme`, `role`, `sequence`);
- `solved.rds` — the whole object: plan, report and the markers themselves.
- `artefact.json` — the manifest: SHA-256 of the reference and the variant
  table, package version and git SHA, every engine version, the design
  parameters, and `overrides` — the knobs that differ from the defaults;
- `decisions.csv` — one row per (target, chemistry) with `outcome`, `verdict`,
  `risk`, the relaxed gates and, for a rejection, the reason the designer gave;
- `checks.csv` — the gate table of the chosen markers;
- `targets.csv` — the loci that were asked for.

The manifest is the part you can argue with. `overrides` is a field of its own
precisely so that a pass obtained under a loosened threshold cannot look like
one obtained under the default, and `marker_replay()` re-runs the design from
`solved.rds` and compares the verdicts instead of asking you to trust them:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
art <- marker_artefact(solved, dir = "results/solved")
art$manifest$overrides        # e.g. min_disc 0.4 against a default of 0.5
replay <- marker_replay(art) # fresh cache: the design runs again
replay$table                  # recorded vs replayed scheme and verdict
replay$inputs_match           # FALSE if the reference was replaced
```

`readRDS()` returns a working object, not a picture: from there you can run
`marker_plot()`, `marker_tubes()` (compatibility of pairs in one tube) and the
checks again without repeating the design:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
back <- readRDS(file.path(dir, "solved.rds"))
identical(back$report$label, solved$report$label)
marker_tubes(back)                      # which pairs can go into one tube
```

If you need the result of **one** assay rather than a panel, it is written by
`write_kasp_results()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_kasp_results(assay, gene, dir = "results")
```

## Why a candidate did not pass

A failure at a locus is an object, not `NULL`. `marker_doomed` prints the stage
at which the candidates ran out, and the reason:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
m <- solved$report$marker[[1]]
inherits(m, "marker_doomed")     # TRUE -> design failed
m$stage                          # "as" or "pair"
m$reason                         # "No AS primer passed the GC/Tm filter."
```

The stages of the KASP pipeline: `as` (allele-specific primers: GC/Tm,
homopolymers/SSR, degenerate 3' code, footprint) → `pair` (the AS × COM pair
after the ladder). The stage in the reason says exactly where the candidates ran
out, not only that "it did not work".

Acceptance checks do not cancel the design: the object is returned, but with the
failures in `$evaluation`. So `marker_doomed` means "there is no marker", while
a failed `marker_assay` means "there is a marker, but it cannot be used without
a decision".

If the object was assembled but with caveats, look at `$selection`. The
relaxation ladder lifts the soft gates one at a time and records what exactly
was lifted:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
assay$selection$relaxed          # which gates were relaxed
assay$selection$violated         # which are still violated
assay$evaluation                 # the checks table saved at assembly
```

An empty `relaxed` and `violated` means the assay passed first time; a non-empty
one means the "least bad" candidate came back, and `cli` warned about it at
assembly.

### The decision policy as text

The decision tree is data: the same gates, tiers and ladder rungs that the
engine sees. The text export can be grepped and works without graphics:

```{r}
txt <- marker_decision_text("snp")
grep("^(==|DOOMED|verdict)", txt, value = TRUE)
```

And inside the section are the concrete thresholds, that is exactly the `limit`
values that `observed` is compared against in the checks table:

```{r}
txt[grep("^== assay acceptance", txt) + seq_len(8)]
```

`plot_decision_tree(scheme = "snp")` draws the same thing as a graph, and
`plot_decision_tree(assay)` draws the path of a particular assay through that
graph (green — applied, amber — relaxed, red — violated).

## On-screen summary

The assay object prints itself compactly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
assay
# <marker_assay> Chr4:269090 G>A (strand -)
#   AS-ref  ...
#   AS-alt  ...
#   COM     ...
#   amplicon 93 bp | discrimination 0.966
```

## Result files

`write_kasp_results()` writes consolidated files:

- `marker_design.csv` — candidate assays (the `discrimination` column is what we rank by);
- `marker_primer_qc.csv` — per primer: `tm`, `gc`, `hairpin_dg`, `terminal_dg`,
  `hits` (3' seed) and `n_products` (in-silico PCR);
- `marker_dimer_dg.csv` — dG of duplexes for all pairs (the diagonal is the homodimer).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
qc <- read.csv("results/marker_primer_qc.csv")
qc[qc$name != "COM" & !is.na(qc$name), , drop = FALSE]   # AS primers
```

## Figures

- `plot_primers()` — the assay map: primers, variant track, toggles;
- `plot_variant_landscape()` — the gene model + an inset of the design region;
- `plot_decision_tree()` — the selection decision tree;
- `marker_plot()` — the "target × chemistry" matrix for a solved plan.

## Profiling: when a run is slow

Design is a grid (strands × lengths × mismatch positions × bases), so "slow"
almost always means "we are building too many objects". The rule is one:
**measure, don't guess**, and write down one testable hypothesis before editing.

```sh
# in the package repository (dev/ is not part of the installed package)
Rscript dev/profile.R run .tmp/probe/solve-one.R .tmp/prof/probe
Rscript dev/profile.R stacks .tmp/prof/probe/probe.out     # analysis without re-running
```

`Rprof` writes a stack per sample, and `dev/profile.R` reads it directly —
`summaryRprof()` aggregates by function name and **hides the caller**, and the
question "who is repeating this?" cannot be answered without the caller. The
output is four files:

| File | What is inside |
|---|---|
| `<name>.out` | the raw profile |
| `<name>.self.csv` | per function: self and total seconds |
| `<name>.frames.csv` | every frame of every stack: depth, function, caller |
| `<name>.rds` | the three tables, for reading again |
| `<name>.ttl` | the same facts as N-Triples (RDF 1.1) |

```{r, eval = FALSE}
source("dev/profile.R")                  # repository only, not in the package
prof <- profile_read(".tmp/prof/probe/probe.out")
profile_report(prof, top = 10)           # the most expensive functions
profile_callers(prof, "CalculateEfficiencyPCR")   # who calls it and how many times
```

What to look for in the table:

- `validObject` / `initialize` / `getClassDef` at the top is **S4 construction**,
  not the algorithm: build fewer objects rather than rewriting the maths;
- the grid multiplies the axes — count how many objects a call builds before
  optimising;
- an expensive path that is discarded anyway must be cut off **before** the grid
  is built (a cheap "doomed" condition first);
- `all.equal()` before and after the edit — otherwise "faster" may mean
  "wrong".

For exchange with other tools (not for debugging) there are tidy and RDF
exports:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tidy <- profile_read_tidy(".tmp/prof/probe/probe.rds")   # three tables, preferred
ttl  <- profile_ttl_read(".tmp/prof/probe/probe.ttl")    # strict N-Triples, error with a line number
```

RDF here is an exchange format: the vocabulary `https://tidymarkers.org/profile#`
(`ProfileRun`, `Function`, `calledBy`) lets the profile be read where there is no
R. Do not debug with it — that is what `Rprof` is for.

And last: `pkgload::load_all()` caches the function body. If behaviour has not
changed after an edit, reload with `recompile = TRUE` before hunting for the bug
in the logic.
